sections.title: Overview
sections.description: Landing summary for the affordability, delay, access, and low-risk story, with income, education, and broad race comparisons surfaced up front.

sections.title: Could Not Afford Care
sections.description: Direct affordability barriers paired with spending, insurance, income, education, and broad race context.

sections.title: Delayed Due To Cost
sections.description: Cost-driven postponement of care, downstream burden patterns, and subgroup differences across the same fairness lenses.

sections.title: Proxy Why They Didn't Buy
sections.description: Proxy-only section using usual source of care and the reason for not having one, clearly separated from direct affordability measures.

sections.title: Can Afford Cohort
sections.description: Requested comparisons inside the cohort reporting no affordability barriers, with income and education framed as descriptive gradients rather than causal drivers.

sections.title: Low-Risk Subsidy Story
sections.description: Acquisition, payer-mix, subgroup equity checks, and scenario sizing using the existing low-risk cohort.

sections.title: Student Lens
sections.description: Ages 17-23 filtered by student status, spending, delay, and low-risk signals.

questions.title: What share could not afford at least one type of care?
questions.howToRead: The donut partitions valid respondents into two groups: those with at least one affordability barrier and those with none across the three care types.

questions.title: Among people who could not afford care, what is annual total spend distribution?
questions.howToRead: Bars show the weighted distribution of annual total spending for the could-not-afford cohort. The median and upper tail reveal how concentrated spending is inside this group.

questions.title: Among people who could not afford care, what is annual out-of-pocket distribution?
questions.howToRead: This histogram isolates annual out-of-pocket spending for the could-not-afford cohort, so high bars in the upper ranges indicate heavier direct financial burden.

questions.title: Are “could not afford” people spending less because they skip care, or more because they are sicker?
questions.howToRead: Use the metric selector to compare distributions for the affordability cohort versus everyone else. Wider boxes or higher medians suggest systematically heavier burden on that metric.

questions.title: Does inability to afford care correlate with being uninsured, public, or private?
questions.howToRead: Each column is one insurance category. The stacked segments show the weighted share with at least one affordability problem versus none.

questions.title: Does inability to afford care vary by poverty category?
questions.howToRead: Read each 100% stacked bar within a poverty band. Taller affordability segments indicate where cost barriers are more common inside that group.

questions.title: How do affordability barriers change across the family income distribution?
questions.howToRead: Bars show the weighted affordability-barrier rate by fixed family-income quintile. Read left to right as a distributional gradient from lower-income to higher-income households.

questions.title: How do affordability barriers shift across education levels?
questions.howToRead: Each bar is the weighted affordability-barrier rate for an adult education band, ordered from less than high school through graduate study to show the education gradient directly.

questions.title: How do affordability barriers vary across broad race groups?
questions.howToRead: Each bar shows the weighted share of a broad race group reporting at least one affordability barrier. Treat this as a descriptive fairness comparison, not a causal explanation.

questions.title: Does inability to afford care vary by employment status?
questions.howToRead: Bars compare weighted affordability-problem rates across adult employment status groups derived from the round 5/3 employment status code.

questions.title: Does inability to afford care vary by age group?
questions.howToRead: The line traces the weighted rate of affordability problems by age band, making it easy to spot where the burden rises or falls across the life course.

questions.title: Does inability to afford care vary by region?
questions.howToRead: Each regional bar shows the weighted affordability-problem rate for that Census region; state coverage for each region appears in tooltips.

questions.title: How many delayed medical care due to cost?
questions.howToRead: The Yes bar estimates people who postponed medical care because of cost; the No bar is the valid remainder.

questions.title: How many delayed dental care due to cost?
questions.howToRead: Use the two weighted bars to compare how many people delayed dental care because of cost versus those who did not.

questions.title: How many delayed prescribed medicine due to cost?
questions.howToRead: This bar chart focuses only on delays in getting prescribed medicine because of cost.

questions.title: What share delayed at least one type due to cost?
questions.howToRead: The donut splits valid respondents into those who delayed at least one care type due to cost and those who did not report any delay.

questions.title: How do delayed-care rates vary across broad race groups?
questions.howToRead: Bars show the weighted delayed-due-to-cost rate within each broad race group. Compare the height of the bars as a descriptive access pattern, not a causal claim.

questions.title: Among people without a usual source of care, what is the main reason?
questions.howToRead: Bars are ranked from the most common to the least common reported reason among people without a usual source of care.

questions.title: What fraction reports “cost of medical care” as the reason for no usual source of care?
questions.howToRead: The donut narrows to the no-USC population only, then splits it between the specific cost-of-medical-care reason and every other reason.

questions.title: For the “cost reason” subgroup, what is the insurance mix?
questions.howToRead: This stacked bar isolates the cost-reason subgroup and shows how it is divided across private, public-only, and uninsured coverage categories.

questions.title: For the “cost reason” subgroup, what are income and poverty levels?
questions.howToRead: The left panel shows poverty categories and the right panel shows fixed family-income quintiles for the cost-reason subgroup.

questions.title: Within the can-afford cohort, how does education shape the spending profile?
questions.howToRead: Each box compares annual total spending inside the can-afford cohort across adult education bands, showing whether lower reported barriers still coexist with different spending profiles.

questions.title: Within the can-afford cohort, how does income shape the spending profile?
questions.howToRead: The boxes compare annual total spending inside the can-afford cohort across income groups, letting you see whether lower reported barriers still mask different levels of healthcare use or cost.

questions.title: Across broad race groups, how does annual total spend differ?
questions.howToRead: Each box shows the annual total-spend distribution for one broad race group. Read differences as descriptive burden patterns within the filtered cohort, not as proof of a race effect.

questions.title: Across broad race groups, how does annual out-of-pocket burden differ?
questions.howToRead: Each box shows annual out-of-pocket spending for one broad race group, so larger medians or upper tails indicate heavier direct financial burden within that group.

questions.title: How does out-of-pocket share change across income quintiles?
questions.howToRead: Each box shows the out-of-pocket share distribution within an income quintile. Lower medians indicate a smaller direct payment share even when people are already using care.

questions.title: How do delayed-due-to-cost rates shift across education levels?
questions.howToRead: Bars show delayed-due-to-cost rates by education band for adults, so you can track whether delay rates fall as educational attainment rises.

questions.title: How do affordability barriers fall as income rises?
questions.howToRead: Read the bars from lower to higher poverty categories to see how affordability barriers taper, persist, or flatten across the income ladder.

questions.title: What fraction of population is low-risk by utilization proxy?
questions.howToRead: The bars compare the weighted population share classified as low risk versus not low risk using the existing precomputed low-risk cohort.

questions.title: What is average annual spend for low-risk vs non-low-risk?
questions.howToRead: Each box captures the annual total-spending distribution for one low-risk class; the comparison shows how separated the two cost profiles are.

questions.title: What is average out-of-pocket for low-risk vs non-low-risk?
questions.howToRead: Use the boxes to compare direct out-of-pocket burden for low-risk versus non-low-risk people.

questions.title: How many uninsured people are low-risk?
questions.howToRead: This chart splits the uninsured-status columns into low-risk and not-low-risk segments so you can size the acquisition opportunity.

questions.title: If low-risk people had lower pricing, how many would be targetable?
questions.howToRead: The funnel starts with the full filtered population, then narrows to low-risk people and finally to the uninsured low-risk segment as a conservative targetable cohort.

questions.title: What is payer mix for the low-risk cohort?
questions.howToRead: The stacked bar divides average spending for the low-risk cohort into private, Medicare, Medicaid, and out-of-pocket components.

questions.title: How does low-risk share vary across broad race groups?
questions.howToRead: Bars show the weighted share classified as low risk within each broad race group. This is a descriptive subgroup comparison to test fairness and acquisition assumptions, not a causal argument.

questions.title: Would focusing only on low-risk uninsured meaningfully expand covered lives?
questions.howToRead: The bars compare three scenario sizes: the entire filtered population, all uninsured people, and the narrower uninsured low-risk group.

questions.title: For ages 17–23, what is affordability profile by student status?
questions.howToRead: Within ages 17-23 only, each student-status bar is split into the share with at least one affordability barrier versus none.

questions.title: For full-time students, what is annual spend and out-of-pocket distribution?
questions.howToRead: The two box plots summarize total annual spending and out-of-pocket spending for full-time students ages 17-23.

questions.title: For full-time students, what is insurance status distribution?
questions.howToRead: This weighted bar chart shows how full-time students split across private, public-only, and uninsured coverage.

questions.title: For full-time students, what share delayed care due to cost?
questions.howToRead: The bars isolate full-time students and show the weighted share that delayed at least one care type due to cost.

questions.title: Are student low-risk signals stronger than non-students in the same age band?
questions.howToRead: Use the metric selector to compare low-risk signals for full-time students versus non-students ages 17-23.

assumptions: Default reporting is weighted with Person weight.
Could-not-afford cohort equals any of Afford medical, Afford dental, or Afford meds coded Yes.
Delayed-due-to-cost cohort equals any of Delay medical, Delay dental, or Delay meds coded Yes.
Can-afford cohort equals No across Afford medical, Afford dental, and Afford meds; mixed valid-and-missing patterns remain unknown for composite cards.
Broad race comparisons use Race group exactly as labeled in the MEPS documentation.
This site frames low-risk and affordability findings as fairness and acquisition exploration, not causal proof.

proxyNotes.no_usc: The no-USC section is a proxy analysis. No-USC reason describes the main reason for not having a usual source of care, not a direct insurance purchase reason.
proxyNotes.low_risk: Low risk is taken from the existing processed low-risk export and used as the primary low-risk cohort for scenario sizing.
proxyNotes.fairness: Income, education, and Race group comparisons are descriptive subgroup views from survey data. They help surface fairness and access patterns, but they do not identify a single causal mechanism.
